title: Turning the Dials
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart challenges the 'lever' model of school improvement, in which leaders imagine that pulling the curriculum, behaviour, quality assurance or wellbeing lever will produce predictable gains, and which tends to produce bloated, RAG-rated improvement plans. Drawing on Matthew Evans, he argues that schools are complex rather than merely complicated systems and proposes a metaphor of interconnected dials, where turning one up can nudge others up or down in ways leaders cannot fully predict. He then separates leadership work into maintenance, which means designing and sustaining habitual systems that keep every dial above a floor, and improvement, which depends above all on growing staff expertise through adult learning. Turning a dial up is recast as shaping conditions: creating opportunities to collaborate, organising accessible learning materials, clarifying strategies, forging shared language and telling stories of success. He concludes that improvement efforts feel busy but brittle when leaders keep correcting dials the system itself knocks out of place, and that schools improve when everyday good work becomes easier and less dependent on individual heroics.
points: Hart argues that treating a school as a set of independent levers produces monstrous improvement plans and staff overload because it ignores the interdependence of a complex system.
The dial metaphor captures side effects, such as a better-sequenced curriculum leaving results flat while depressing teacher wellbeing through extra resourcing workload.
He splits leadership work into maintenance (habitual systems that stop any dial slipping) and improvement (deliberately raising staff expertise), which is the only real route to better outcomes.
Turning a dial is defined as shaping conditions, including collaboration time, accessible materials, clarified strategies, shared language and storytelling, rather than issuing directives.
His closing claim is that coherence comes from thoughtful design and sustained learning rather than urgency or enforcement, so improvement should reduce reliance on individual heroics.
quotes: It is tempting to believe that if we just pull the curriculum lever, we’ll get better results. If we just pull the behaviour lever, we’ll get fewer incidents. If we just pull the quality assurance lever, we can really drive up standards.

These are examples still of the school as a complicated system, not a complex one. When we pull the teaching lever, or the parental engagement lever, or the marking lever, they won’t just have an effect on the thing that we might want it to, but on all sorts of other things, some of which we might be able to predict and some of which we absolutely cannot.

Let’s say we turn the curriculum dial up and our curriculum is objectively more intelligently sequenced. This might not nudge the results dial at all! And it might even nudge the teacher wellbeing dial down because of the increased workload of resourcing a revamped curriculum.

As Matthew Evans argues, and I wholeheartedly agree, there can be no school improvement, no improvement in any of those objects, without greater staff expertise. And how do we increase staff expertise? By setting our school up to prioritise adult learning.
Turning a dial then is about shaping the conditions in which better work becomes more likely. It is about reducing friction and creating the space in which professional expertise can grow.
This is why so many school improvement efforts feel busy but brittle. We spend huge amounts of energy adjusting dials that are constantly being knocked out of place by the system itself.

Schools do not improve because leaders turn the right dial at the right moment. They improve when the everyday work of teaching and learning becomes easier to do well, more likely to happen and less dependent on individual heroics.
